stem: An obese patient just finished day surgery in the morning for right inguinal hernia repair. In the recovery room the patient has a fever and is in severe pain. The wound and surrounding area all the way down to the thigh is red, tender with areas of discolouration and crepitus. What do you do?

opts.t: Broad spectrum Antibiotic and immediate surgical debridement
Broad spectrum antibiotic and consult ID

expl: Severe pain, redness spreading to the thigh, discoloration and crepitus within hours of surgery = necrotizing infection → antibiotics + immediate debridement.

stem: A 22-year-old healthy patient is scheduled for a splenectomy due to hypersplenism. Which of the following is the best intervention to reduce the risk of future infections?

opts.t: Vaccination against Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae type B

expl: Splenectomy removes protection against encapsulated organisms → vaccinate against S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis and H. influenzae b (ideally ≥2 weeks before elective surgery).

why.D: Used in selected high-risk patients (e.g. children), not the best single intervention.

stem: 24 yo female who underwent excision of lipoma on the left lateral thigh. Now she presented with severe pain in her left thigh enabling her from ambulation, her pain associated with high fever, erythema, swelling and crepitus. It's also associated with bullae and bruising. She noticed that the colour of her thigh is rapidly changing to darker. Which of the following is the next step?

opts.t: Admission to icu with septic screening
Broad spectrum ABx with urgent surgical debridement.

expl: Severe pain, fever, bullae, bruising, crepitus and rapidly darkening skin after minor surgery = necrotizing fasciitis. Treatment is a surgical emergency: broad-spectrum antibiotics plus urgent debridement.

why.A: Antibiotics alone don't penetrate necrotic tissue; mortality rises with delay.
why.B: This is not an allergic reaction.
why.C: ICU care may be needed, but surgery must not be delayed.

stem: A female patient had surgery 2 days ago. She had severe pain that limited ambulation. Now she has a fever of 40.2 C. What is the most likely cause?
expl: Fever on post-op day 2 with pain limiting deep breathing/ambulation is classically atelectasis (UTI, SSI and pneumonia come later).

stem: A 35-year-old man with 40% body surface area burns was admitted to the ICU. He was intubated for airway protection, a central venous catheter was inserted, and he was started on total parenteral nutrition. After one week, he developed high-grade fever and leukocytosis. What is the most common ICU infection in burn patients?
expl: An intubated ICU patient's commonest infection is ventilator-associated pneumonia (the slides: most common surgical infection in ICU).

why.B: CLABSI is common but less than VAP.

stem: A patient underwent a controlled colectomy and before closure they did irrigation. What type of surgery is this?
expl: A controlled opening of the bowel (elective colectomy) without spillage is clean-contaminated; irrigation doesn't change the class.

why.A: Clean means no hollow viscus entered.

stem: A 45-year-old woman undergoes emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis. During surgery, there is no perforation, no pus, and no bile spillage into the peritoneum, What is the wound classification of this operation?
expl: Cholecystectomy enters the biliary tract in a controlled way. With no perforation, pus or bile spillage it stays clean-contaminated even as an emergency.

stem: A 65-year-old patient is on postoperative day 3 receiving broad-spectrum antibiotics. He develops mild abdominal pain and watery diarrhea. Vital signs are stable, and there are no signs of severe infection. Stool tests confirm Clostridium difficile infection (CDI). What is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: Give oral vancomycin or oral fidaxomicin

expl: Non-severe C. difficile infection is treated with oral vancomycin or oral fidaxomicin (and stopping the offending antibiotic when possible).

why.A: Helpful but not sufficient treatment alone.
why.B: IV vancomycin doesn't reach the colon.

stem: A 60-year-old patient is postoperative on day 2. He has tachycardia (HR 110), tachypnea (RR 25), temperature 38.5°C, blood pressure 120/75 mmHg, and WBC 13,000. Which of the following is the most appropriate classification?
expl: SIRS = ≥2 of: T >38/<36, HR >90, RR >20, WBC >12k/<4k. He has all four, normal BP and no organ dysfunction.

why.A: These numbers exceed the normal post-op response.

stem: A 50-year-old patient is postoperative day 5 after abdominal surgery. He develops purulent discharge from the surgical site but is hemodynamically stable, afebrile, and has no systemic symptoms. What is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: Return to the operating room for debridement
Open and clean the wound at the bedside, change dressings regularly

expl: A superficial SSI with pus in a stable, afebrile patient → open the wound, clean, and dress regularly (drainage is the treatment).

why.A: OR debridement is for deep/necrotizing infection.
why.B: IV antibiotics are not needed without systemic signs.

stem: A 65-year-old patient is postoperative day 2 after abdominal surgery. He develops tachycardia, hypotension, fever, and cold extremities, with elevated lactate, Bedside point-of-care ultrasound shows a collapsed inferior vena cava (IVC) and a hyperdynamic left ventricle. Which of the following best describes the underlying pathophysiology of his condition?

opts.t: Systemic vasodilation with decreased systemic vascular resistance (SVR)

expl: Fever + hypotension with a hyperdynamic LV and collapsed IVC = distributive (septic) shock from systemic vasodilation and low SVR.

why.A: Pump failure would give a poor LV and full IVC.
why.B: Hypovolemia gives a collapsed IVC too, but fever and a hyperdynamic heart point to sepsis.

stem: A patient develops fever 48 hours after surgery. What is the most likely cause?
expl: Classic teaching: fever within 48 h after surgery is most often atelectasis (the "5 Ws": wind, water, wound, walking, wonder drugs).

stem: Fecal spillage in the OR. What class of wounds?
expl: Gross spillage of bowel content = contaminated wound (class 3).

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with fever, altered mental status. BP was 80/50 mmHg, MAP 55. He is tachycardic (HR 120 bpm) and febrile (39.2°C). Labs show elevated creatinine (2.5 mg/dL), LDH (500 U/L), and lactate (4.5 mmol/L). What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Fever, confusion, hypotension (MAP 55), raised creatinine and lactate 4.5 = septic shock.

why.C: May be the source, but the picture is septic shock.
why.D: No bleeding described; fever points to sepsis.

stem: A patient presents on day 3 post-operation with fever, local abdominal tenderness, erythema, and purulent discharge from the wound. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Fever, local tenderness, erythema and purulent wound discharge on day 3 = surgical site infection.

why.C: Dehiscence = wound separation with serosanguinous fluid.

stem: 19 y/o present to the ER with perforated appendicitis and we did laparoscopic appendectomy with multiple time wash the abdomen we discharge the patient and he present later with persistent fever with RLQ tenderness without sign of peritonitis HR and blood pressure is normal WBC is 14 after doing CT we found 6 CM RLQ collection what is the best management?
expl: A stable patient with a 6 cm well-defined abscess → antibiotics + image-guided percutaneous drainage (less invasive than surgery).

why.A: Surgery is for failed percutaneous drainage or peritonitis.
why.D: Antibiotics alone don't drain a large collection.

stem: A 50 year old man did surgery a couple of days ago, currently in the ICU unable to wean from the ventilator, although he was successfully extubated after surgery. You suspect the patient has SIRS (Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome) which of the following supports your diagnosis?
expl: Temperature >38 and WBC >12,000 are two SIRS criteria.

stem: A 50 years old man did surgery a couple of days ago, currently in the ICU unable to wean from the ventilator, although he was successfully extubated after surgery. You suspect the patient has SIRS (Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome) which of the following supports your diagnosis?
expl: Source key: gastroduodenal (stress) ulcer — a recognized consequence of the systemic stress response/SIRS in ICU patients. The question is poorly recalled.

why.A: An NG tube doesn't support SIRS.
why.D: Renal injury would suggest organ dysfunction (sepsis), not SIRS.

stem: Your patient is being prepared to undergo an elective Sigmoidectomy. What is the Category of the surgical wound?
expl: Elective sigmoid colectomy = controlled entry into the colon → clean-contaminated.

stem: Patient went for elective Thyroidectomy for thyroid cancer, what is the type?
expl: Thyroidectomy doesn't enter a hollow viscus → clean.

stem: A 55 y/o man who is receiving total parenteral nutrition through the right subclavian PICC for short bowel syndrome developed high temperature (39C). Two blood cultures were positive for staphylococcus aureus. Which of the following is the most appropriate step in management?

opts.t: Remove the PICC, send tip for culture and administer antibiotics
Change the PICC over the wire

expl: S. aureus bacteremia from a central line (PICC) → remove the line (send the tip for culture) and give a long antibiotic course. S. aureus is never a contaminant.

why.B: Exchanging over a wire keeps an infected tract.
why.C: Lock therapy isn't enough for S. aureus.

stem: A 68 y/o woman was admitted through the ER with an abscess in the right foot. She underwent surgical drainage of the abscess with an intravenous therapeutic course of Cefuxime. Five days later. She developed diarrhea with mucus. Which of the following organisms is the most likely underlying cause of the diarrhea?
srcNote: Source note (431 A Q53): pseudomembranous colitis
expl: Diarrhea after a course of a cephalosporin = C. difficile (pseudomembranous colitis).

stem: Diabetic patient removed lipoma suture with pain and erythema at site but otherwise normal how to deal with this patient
expl: Source key: proper hand hygiene — the most effective infection-prevention measure. Mild erythema without systemic illness doesn't need antibiotics.

why.A: Not needed for mild local signs.
why.D: Reasonable care, but hand hygiene is keyed.

stem: A case about a patient who has done a successful non-complicated laparoscopic appendectomy, and asked about how to prevent surgical infections in this patient ?

opts.t: Pre-op cefazolin, during the surgery, and for 72 hours post-op

expl: For uncomplicated appendicitis/appendectomy, a peri-operative dose of a cephalosporin + metronidazole (covers gut aerobes and anaerobes) is enough; no prolonged post-op course.

why.A: Cefazolin lacks anaerobic cover and 72 hours post-op is unnecessary.

stem: A question about how to prevent ventilator acquired pneumonia in an ICU patient ?

opts.t: daily extubation and daily trial to remove it as soon as possible

expl: VAP prevention bundle: daily sedation interruption and spontaneous breathing trials to extubate early, head-of-bed elevation 30–45°, oral care.

why.A: The head should be raised, not lowered.
why.C: Daily sedation holds are part of the bundle.

stem: A 32 year old man presented with ruptured appendicitis. A Laparoscopic procedure was done. 4 days post-op, he had a fever and and a right lower quadrant pain, but the wound looked OK with no redness or discharge. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Fever and RLQ pain on day 4 after appendectomy for a ruptured appendix with a normal wound = intra-abdominal (pelvic/RLQ) abscess — an organ-space SSI.

why.A: Cecal perforation/leak would give peritonitis and sepsis.

stem: A patient post laparotomy presents after 6 days with pain and erythema at site no fever no discharge and otherwise what is the best way to manage this patient?
expl: Pain and erythema without fever or discharge = superficial wound problem → local care (daily cleansing).

stem: A 36 year old man presented with swelling in his nape, as well as erythema and pus from multiple sites. What is the most likely diagnosis
expl: A carbuncle is a group of infected hair follicles (often on the nape/back, in diabetics) discharging pus from multiple openings.

why.A: A furuncle is a single follicle with one opening.
why.B: A sebaceous cyst has a punctum, not multiple openings.

stem: A 65 y/o man who is receiving total parenteral nutrition for high output small bowel fistula with persistent hyperglycemia inspite of insulin infusion. Which of the following is the appropriate step in management?
expl: New, persistent hyperglycemia on TPN despite insulin often signals hidden sepsis — look for the source.

why.A: Oral agents are irrelevant on TPN.

stem: Patient with variceal bleeding after the initial maintenance of airway, breathing, and circulation. Which intravenous medication has been shown to reduce the mortality incidence in this case?
expl: In variceal bleeding (cirrhosis), prophylactic antibiotics (ceftriaxone) reduce infection, rebleeding and mortality.

why.A: Octreotide controls bleeding but its mortality benefit is less established.

stem: a patient presented after a trauma with splenic rupture. He had a splenectomy. A year later he presented with hypotension, fever, and septic shock. What is the most likely organism?
expl: After splenectomy, overwhelming post-splenectomy infection is caused by encapsulated organisms — mostly Streptococcus pneumoniae.

stem: Tight control of sugar level in a diabetic patient undergoing surgery:

opts.t: Decrease the incidence of deep wound infection

expl: Tight peri-operative glucose control lowers surgical-site (deep wound) infection.

why.B: Not a benefit of glucose control.
why.C: Phagocytosis improves, but the tested outcome is fewer infections.
why.D: Wrong — glucose control clearly improves outcomes.

stem: In general precautions, which of the following should be avoided?

opts.t: Sharp instruments discarded in special sharp container
Drapes should be placed in containers
Needles should be resheathed by the same person
Gloves and gown should be removed after all used equipment

srcNote: (Patient safety) (practical procedures & investigations of surgical patients)
expl: Re-sheathing (re-capping) needles is the classic cause of needle-stick injury and must be avoided; sharps go straight into a sharps container.

why.A: This is correct practice, not something to avoid.

stem: A pt with progressive swelling in his leg for 2 days presented with severe pain and black blisters, what is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Rapid progression, pain out of proportion and haemorrhagic/black bullae (skin necrosis) = necrotizing fasciitis → urgent debridement.

stem: A 72-year-old lady who has diabetes and hypertension underwent elective cystoscopy due to obstructive uropathy causing urinary tract infection (UTI). A few days later, she presented to the Emergency Department with altered level of consciousness, hypotension, tachycardia, and high fever. She was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) and required intubation for a few days. She received multiple courses of broad-spectrum antibiotics during her hospital stay for 3 weeks. When assessed for discharge, she had no signs or symptoms of infection. A review of her chart revealed a recent positive blood culture growing Staphylococcus Epidermidis in a single sample. What is the best next step in the management of this patient?

opts.t: Repeat blood cultures and keep the patient admitted until the results come out
Repeat cystoscopy, and get blood and urine cultures

expl: A single positive culture of S. epidermidis (coagulase-negative staph) in a well patient is most likely a skin contaminant → discharge as planned.

why.B: Not needed when she is well.

stem: Scenario about diabetic patient who undergo resection of lipoma came after with mild pain in the surgical area , examination show erythematous edge and pain , (removal of suture showed no pus (similar) the remaining of question was excluding abscess) what is the diagnosis?
expl: Erythema and mild pain without pus after a lipoma excision = superficial skin infection (cellulitis of the wound edge).

why.C: Suture allergy isn't the classic answer.

stem: Which of the following is considered a high-risk surgical procedure for infection?

opts.t: Resection of lower part of the lung

expl: A traumatic tracheoesophageal fistula is contaminated/dirty (aerodigestive contamination) — the highest infection risk among the options.

stem: a long scenario of a patient which has been stabbed in the abdomen and he is stable with Intestinal evisceration. Which of the following is the antibiotic of choice to prevent surgical site infection?
expl: Penetrating abdominal trauma with evisceration → bowel flora prophylaxis covering gram-negatives and anaerobes: ceftriaxone + metronidazole.

stem: A patient with lipoma in the back 3-4 cm came and you took the lipoma out, a month later he came in with pain at the site of injury and erythema around the wound with no discharge or abscess. What is the management?
expl: Pain and erythema a month after surgery without discharge or abscess → superficial problem → local wound care.

stem: A patient scheduled for abdominal aortic aneurysm repair with synthetic graft. He is allergic to penicillin. Which antibiotic prophylaxis should you give the patient ?
expl: Prosthetic graft surgery needs anti-staphylococcal prophylaxis. With penicillin allergy, use clindamycin (or vancomycin) instead of cefazolin.

why.A: Cefazolin is avoided in significant penicillin allergy; metronidazole isn't needed.
why.D: Cefepime is a broad treatment agent, not prophylaxis.

stem: A 29- year old man presented to the Emergency department with acute appendicitis. He underwent an uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy. What is the most effective measure to prevent a surgical infection in this patient?

opts.t: Transition from IV abx to oral

expl: Hand hygiene is the single most effective infection-prevention measure.

stem: A 35-year-old man came to the emergency department complaining of persistent hiccups. He had undergone sleeve gastrectomy 10 days ago. His vital signs were HR: 112,BP 99/60, 02 Sat 99% on Room Air, Temp: 39C What is the best next step in his management following resuscitation?

opts.t: Reassure patient that hiccups are expected and will go away
Consult pulmonology to manage his hiccups
Obtain a CT scan of the abdomen to rule out leak or abscess
Prescribe chlorpromazine and discharge the patient

expl: Fever, tachycardia and hiccups (diaphragmatic irritation) after sleeve gastrectomy suggest a staple-line leak/subphrenic abscess → CT abdomen.

stem: You were consulted to see a 56-years-old female who has been admitted to the hospital for 3 weeks. You got called because she is complaining of redness and swelling with pus coming out of the IV site. You sent the pus for culture and sensitivity. What is your next course of action?

opts.t: Remove the line and resect the vein
Start patient on IV antibiotics and NSAIDS
Start the patient on oral antibiotics and IV heparin
Remove the IV line and start antibiotics

expl: Pus at an IV site = infected line (suppurative thrombophlebitis) → remove the line and start antibiotics (guided by culture). Vein excision is only for persistent suppurative thrombophlebitis.

why.A: Excision is reserved for failure of treatment.
why.B: Leaving the line in keeps the source.
why.C: Line must be removed; heparin isn't routine.

stem: What is the most common cause of catheter associated UTI?
expl: Source key: improper catheterization technique. Most CAUTIs arise from organisms entering along the catheter — breaks in aseptic insertion and catheter care, and long duration.

why.A: The route, but not the keyed answer.

stem: A 60 man presented to ER unconscious after he had a laceration in his arm when he was cleaning his grass cutter. His wound had mud, oil, soil, and grass. His wife doesn't recall if he ever received the tetanus vaccine before. What is the next step of management?

opts.t: Give antibiotic with delayed administration of toxoid vaccine
Give toxoid vaccine and toxoid immunoglobulin

expl: A tetanus-prone (dirty) wound with unknown or <3 previous doses → give tetanus toxoid AND tetanus immunoglobulin (passive immunity now, active for the future), plus wound care.

why.A: Delaying the toxoid leaves him unprotected.
why.C: Not enough for a dirty wound with unknown status.

stem: Young man presented to ER with right leg cellulitis. Upon starting IV Penicillin G he had shortness of breath and BP became lower and pulse 43 bpm. What is the initial step?
expl: Anaphylaxis to penicillin: the first step is to stop the offending drug, then airway, adrenaline and fluids.

why.B: Next (after stopping the trigger) if the airway is compromised.
why.C: Part of treatment after stopping the drug.

stem: Pt. with PICC line. His infection is not responding to abx. what to do next?
expl: A line infection that doesn't respond to antibiotics → remove the PICC (source control).

why.B: Changing antibiotics doesn't remove the infected device.

stem: A 32-year-old man underwent open appendectomy for perforated appendicitis. He was started on therapeutic course of intravenous Cefuroxime and metronidazole. Five days later, the wound became painful, swollen, red with pus discharge. Which of the following is the most appropriate step in management?
srcNote: (Surgical Infections) Source note (432 F Q53): drain it
expl: Pus in a wound = an abscess that needs drainage — open the wound. Changing/increasing antibiotics doesn't treat pus.

stem: A 51 years old male underwent exploratory laparotomy 3 weeks ago. Patient presented to the ER with right epigastric pain for 2 weeks. Patient was febrile (38.8) and with high WBCs (18,000) CT abdomen showed large intra-abdominal collection (12*18 cm ) what is the most appropriate next step ?
expl: A large intra-abdominal collection after laparotomy → image-guided percutaneous drainage first (compilers marked "not sure").

why.D: Reserved for failed drainage or peritonitis.

stem: 67 y\o man admitted for investigations of liver mass. During admission he developed urinary tract infection.Which of the following best describe this type of infection?
srcNote: Source note (429 F Q15): infection acquired after hospitalization)
expl: An infection acquired during hospitalization (>48 h after admission) = nosocomial.

why.A: Superinfection = a new infection on top of an existing one.

stem: Which of the following is part of SIRs?
expl: SIRS criteria = temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, WBC.

stem: A 25 y\o patient came to ED with a history of diffuse abdominal pain for 4 days. Physical examination revealed diffuse abdominal distention and tenderness with sluggish bowel sounds. Laboratory values showed: WBC 21*109/l, with normal amylase. He underwent exploratory laparotomy and found to have perforated duodenal ulcer with diffuse peritoneal soiling with purulent material. Temperature: 39. Blood pressure: 85\50 mmHg. Pulse: 125 beat\min Which of the following characterize the shock state of this patient?
srcNote: Source note (429 F Q1): septic shock, Infection triggers a cytokine-mediated proinflammatory response that results in peripheral vasodilation, redistribution of blood flow, endothelial cell activation, increased vascular permeability and the formation of microthrombi within the microcirculation. Cardiac output typically increases in septic shock to compensate for the peripheral vasodilation. However, despite a global increase in oxygen delivery, microcirculatory dysfunction impairs oxygen delivery to the cells. Compounding disturbances in oxygen delivery, mitochondrial dysfunction blocks the normal bioenergetic pathways within the cell impairing oxygen utilization. Davidson page number 18, chapter one
expl: Septic shock from purulent peritonitis: cytokines cause peripheral vasodilation, with compensatory high cardiac output.

why.C: Also seen in early sepsis, but the keyed defining feature is vasodilation.

stem: Patient with fever and tachycardia with normal BP but high WBC in urine and high urea and creatinine , MAP= 75 .. what is it ?
srcNote: ( because there is organ damage ) Source figure: 432 F Q61
expl: Old terminology: SIRS + infection = sepsis; sepsis + organ dysfunction (raised urea/creatinine) = severe sepsis; with hypotension unresponsive to fluids = septic shock. MAP 75 is not shock.

why.A: There is infection and organ dysfunction.

stem: 68 year old female had hypovolemic shock due to splenic rupture and underwent splenectomy, and was transfused 8 packed RBCs. 3 days post op she started to have fever (38.2) blood culture showed gram negative bacilli what is the most likely cause of her bacteraemia?
srcNote: Source note (432 F Q4): “As described above, the redistribution of cardiac output observed in shock leads to a marked reduction in splanchnic blood flow. In the stomach, the resulting mucosal hypoperfusion and hypoxia predispose to stress ulceration and haemorrhage. In the intestine, movement (translocation) of bacteria and/or bacterial endotoxin from the lumen to the portal vein and then systemic circulation is thought to be a key mechanism underlying the development of SIRS and multiple organ failure” -Davidsons page 22
expl: Shock reduces splanchnic perfusion → gut mucosal ischemia → bacteria/endotoxin translocate into the portal and systemic circulation → gram-negative bacteremia.

why.B: Possible but not the keyed mechanism.

stem: A 40 year old diabetic patient who had a trauma and ended with deep laceration of his right arm which was sutured 8 hrs after the accident. The patient presented to the emergency 5 days afterwards with redness and pus discharge from the wound. We have opened and irrigated the wound and put it on a regular dressing. What is the expected change in the wound healing process?
expl: An infected wound opened and left to heal by secondary intention → the inflammatory phase is prolonged and the proliferative phase (granulation, contraction, epithelialization) takes longer.

why.C: Collagen is still made (more of it, slower).

stem: A 25 y/o admitted through emergency department complaining of right iliac fossa pain for 5 days. Physical examination revealed tenderness and fullness in right iliac fossa. Ultrasound showed acute appendicitis with significant pus collection in right iliac fossa. Temperature: 38.5 0C, BP; 80/40, Pulse: 115/min. Which of the following is the definitive step in management of this patient?
expl: Resuscitation and antibiotics come first, but the DEFINITIVE treatment of an abscess is drainage (source control).

stem: Therapeutic course of antibiotics is indicated in which of the following procedure?

opts.t: Inguinal hernia repair with mesh implant

expl: A therapeutic (not prophylactic) course is given for established infection — perforated appendicitis (dirty wound).

stem: A 52 y/o diabetic man sustained trauma to right heel injury 7 days ago. Presented to emergency department with pain and swelling of right foot and leg. Physical examination revealed edema, skin discoloration crepitus of right foot and leg. Temperature: 39.50C. What is the most likely cause for this complaint?
srcNote: (Surgical Infections) Source note (430 A Q69): crepitus means air under the skin think the cause is anerobic bacteria
expl: Crepitus (gas in tissue), discoloration and high fever after a wound in a diabetic → gas gangrene (Clostridium perfringens).

stem: 40 y\o woman presented with progressive redness over the dorsum of left hand. Associated with pain and fever. She gave history of knife prick at affected area 3 days ago. Which of the following if the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: (Surgical Infections) Source note (429 F Q23): (progressive + inflammation)
expl: Progressive erythema, pain and fever after a skin breach = cellulitis (no crepitus or necrosis).

why.A: Would show severe pain, bullae, necrosis.

stem: A 41 y/o man admitted through emergency department complaining of right upper quadrant abdominal pain with yellowish discoloration of sclera, dark urine and fever for 5 days. On examination he was jaundiced with pulse rate of 122/min and blood pressure of 85/45 mmHg. Laboratory values showed high liver function test with dilated biliary tree in the ultrasound. Diagnosis of acute toxic cholangitis was made. Which one of the following characterizes the condition of this patient?
expl: Toxic (suppurative) cholangitis with shock = septic shock; at the cell level there is microcirculatory dysfunction impairing oxygen delivery.

stem: A 46 y/o diabetic man admitted through emergency department with diagnosis of ascending cholangitis. He was started on therapeutic course of intravenous amoxicillin, metronidazole and gentamicin. Three days later the serum urea and creatinine steadily elevated. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?
expl: Gentamicin is nephrotoxic; a rising creatinine means stop it (and switch to a non-nephrotoxic agent).

stem: 35 y\o male who is 5 days post appendectomy complained of pain redness and swelling of operation site with some purulent discharge. He has fever. Which of the following is the most appropriate step in management?
expl: Infected wound with pus → remove sutures and drain.

why.B: Not the standard approach for a superficial wound abscess.

stem: A 50 y/o man known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, presented progressive painful swelling with multiple discharging openings on his back.Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Painful swelling with multiple discharging sinuses on the back in a diabetic = carbuncle.

stem: Which of the following is the commonest organism in the large bowel?
expl: Bacteroides (anaerobes) are the most numerous organisms in the colon.

why.A: Not a normal colonic dominant organism.

stem: 27 y\o woman sustained cut wound over lateral aspect of right leg, 2 days later she developed redness, swelling, hotness and tenderness over the same area.Which of the following antibiotics is indicated in the treatment?
srcNote: ( Surgical infections ) Source note (429 F Q41): Dx: cellulitis.
expl: Cellulitis after a cut → strep/staph; the old key chose penicillin G (streptococcal cellulitis).

stem: Which of the following is appropriate initial management of diabetic patient who present with tetanus due to traumatic wound in right foot?
srcNote: ( Trauma ) Source note (429 F Q51): Treatment of tetanus is best performed in the intensive care unit in consultation with an anesthesiologist or critical care specialist trained in the management of the complications of this disease, including early and aggressive airway management. The goals of treatment include: Halting the toxin production, Neutralization of the unbound toxin, Airway management, Control of muscle spasms, Management of dysautonomia and General supportive management. UpToDate
expl: Tetanus kills by laryngospasm and respiratory failure → secure the airway/ventilation first, then immunoglobulin, debridement and antibiotics.

stem: A 70 y/o male patient, 6 days post-elective surgery, was brought to the emergency department with decreased level of consciousness. On examination he appears flushed and his extremities are (something ... Couldn’t remember) touch. His pulse 120/min, BP: 70/45 and oxygen saturation is 96% on 4L O2. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Flushed warm skin, hypotension, tachycardia and altered consciousness after surgery → septic (distributive) shock (compilers "not sure").

why.B: Cardiogenic shock gives cold, clammy extremities.

stem: A 30 y/o man is admitted to surgery department for huge abscess drainage. He was started on antibiotics and analgesics, but complains of sudden severe shortness of breath. There is no chest pain, but he is cyanosed and there was diffuse wheezing over the chest. His BP: 70/30 mmHg and HR is … tachycardic ? couldn’t remember. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: ? Mostly because after the administration of antibiotics he developed these symptoms
expl: Sudden dyspnea, diffuse wheeze, cyanosis and hypotension right after starting antibiotics = anaphylaxis.

stem: A 17 y/o boy was operated for a perforated appendix and was discharged after 5 days in good condition. He came to emergency room 3 days later complaining of mild fever, pain and discharge at the surgical site. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management of this complication?

opts.t: Give oral antibiotics, reassurance and send home.

expl: Pain, mild fever and discharge at the wound after appendectomy = superficial SSI → open the wound.

why.B: Not needed for a superficial infection.

stem: 60 y/o man who is known to have diabetic, hypertension, congenital hyperbilirubin and spherocytosis, was admitted for investigation of abdominal mass which was proved to be mesenteric cyst. He was operated on day 9. 4 days later he developed a surgical site infection. Which of the following is significantly increase the risk of wound infection in this patient?
expl: Diabetes impairs neutrophil function and healing → significantly increases SSI risk.

why.D: Mild anemia isn't the key factor.

stem: Which of the following is the appropriate antibiotics regimen for a patient undergoing appendectomy?
srcNote: (Surgical infections). to cover gram negative , gram positive, bacteroides or anaerobes Source figure: 429 F Q24
expl: Appendectomy prophylaxis must cover gram-negative rods and anaerobes (Bacteroides): a cephalosporin + metronidazole.

why.C: Clindamycin + metronidazole duplicates anaerobic cover and misses gram-negatives.

stem: A 50-year-old woman is admitted with colicky central abdominal pain, and passing blood Stained diarrhea, and mucus per rectum. She had a marked fever and tachycardia. Abdominal plain film radiography appears normal.The white cell count is raised and stool analysis revealed the presence of clostridium difficile cytotoxins. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Colitis with fever, bloody mucoid diarrhoea and C. difficile toxin in stool = pseudomembranous colitis.

stem: blood transfusion can transmit which of the following infection:
expl: Hepatitis B (and C, HIV) is transmitted by blood. Hepatitis A is fecal–oral; hepatitis D needs HBV.

why.C: Needs co-infection with B; B is the classic answer.

stem: laparoscopic Cholecystectomy wound is which type of surgical wound classification?
expl: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy enters the biliary tract in a controlled way → clean-contaminated (type 2).
